Buckler
BUK-ler
n.
From Old French bocler, “shield with a boss”; a small round shield held in the hand. In the KJV, used for several Hebrew words for shield (mágēn, tsinnāh, sōchērāh); especially significant in the Psalms where the LORD Himself is named the saint’s buckler.

📖 Biblical Definition

The buckler in the KJV is a small round shield used in close combat—distinct from the larger body-shield (the thureos of Ephesians 6:16 rendered shield) but serving the same defensive function. The Hebrew terms behind buckler (chiefly mágēn, also tsinnāh and sōchērāh) cover both larger shields and smaller hand-shields; the KJV translators chose to render some uses as buckler to preserve the distinction from the larger shield. The supreme biblical use is the divine-protection imagery of the Psalms, where the LORD Himself is repeatedly named the saint’s buckler. Psalm 18:2: the LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower. Psalm 18:30: as for God, his way is perfect: the word of the LORD is tried: he is a buckler to all those that trust in him. Psalm 35:2: take hold of shield and buckler, and stand up for mine help. Psalm 91:4: he shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler. Proverbs 2:7: he layeth up sound wisdom for the righteous: he is a buckler to them that walk uprightly. The doctrine is consistent across these uses: the LORD Himself is the saint’s personal defensive armor; the buckler-imagery names the close-combat defensive protection the LORD provides for the saint’s individual battles. Several structural features mark the doctrine. First, the LORD’s personal defensive presence: not the LORD provides a buckler or the LORD authorizes a buckler, but the LORD is a buckler. The protection is His own person, applied to the saint in the saint’s particular circumstances. Second, the trust-conditional: the LORD is a buckler to those that trust in him (Ps 18:30); to them that walk uprightly (Prov 2:7). The buckler-protection is appropriated by trust; the believer who does not trust does not receive the defensive coverage the LORD’s personal presence offers. Third, the close-combat appropriateness: a buckler is for close combat, where the enemy is at hand and the defensive protection must be immediately deployable. The Psalmic imagery suits the saint’s actual experience of close-combat spiritual warfare—the immediate threats, the personal attacks, the day-to-day pressures—where the LORD’s close defensive presence is exactly the protection needed. Fourth, the relation to the armor-of-God shield. The NT armor-of-God includes the shield of faith (Eph 6:16), the body-shield by which the saint quenches the fiery darts of the wicked. The OT buckler is the close-combat cousin: the saint’s defense in the immediate close-quarter assault, with the LORD Himself as the buckler. Both the larger shield-of-faith and the personal-presence buckler defend the saint; together they constitute the comprehensive defensive protection the spiritual warfare requires.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BUCKLER as a small round shield used in close combat; in scripture, applied repeatedly to the LORD Himself as the saint’s personal defensive presence (Ps 18:2, 30; 91:4; Prov 2:7): the close-combat divine protection appropriated by trust in the LORD who is Himself the buckler.

expand to see more

BUCKLER, n. — A kind of shield, or piece of defensive armor, used to defend the head, breast or other parts of the body, by warding off attacks. His truth shall be thy shield and buckler (Psa 91:4).

SHIELD, n. — A broad piece of defensive armor; in scripture, both the larger body-shield (the shield of faith in Eph 6:16) and the smaller hand-shield (the buckler of the Psalms).

📖 Key Scripture

Psalm 18:2 — "The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower."

Psalm 91:4 — "He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler."

Proverbs 2:7 — "He layeth up sound wisdom for the righteous: he is a buckler to them that walk uprightly."

2 Samuel 22:31 — "As for God, his way is perfect; the word of the LORD is tried: he is a buckler to all them that trust in him."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The buckler-doctrine is corrupted chiefly by the modernization that has dropped buckler from contemporary English vocabulary (substituting generic shield and losing the close-combat distinction)—and by the general loss of the LORD-Himself-as-defensive-armor register in much contemporary preaching, which has reduced divine protection to abstract general providence without the personal-immediate-presence imagery the Psalmic buckler-references intend.

expand to see more

The modernization has dropped buckler from contemporary English vocabulary almost entirely, with the result that modern translations render the various Hebrew shield-terms uniformly as shield, losing the close-combat distinction the KJV preserved. The loss is small in vocabulary but real in nuance. The KJV’s shield-and-buckler pairing (Ps 91:4: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler) conveys the comprehensive defensive coverage—both the larger body-shield and the close-combat hand-shield together. The recovery is the recovery of attention to the KJV’s careful vocabulary, which often preserves distinctions the modernizations have flattened.

The deeper loss is the LORD-Himself-as-defensive-armor register that the Psalmic buckler-references repeatedly use. The Psalmist does not say God provides a buckler or God appoints my buckler; he says the LORD is my buckler—the protection is the LORD’s own personal presence, applied to the saint’s individual circumstances. The contemporary preaching that has reduced divine protection to abstract general providence (God watches over you, God is taking care of you) loses the personal-immediate-presence imagery the Psalmic buckler-references intend. The recovery is the recovery of the substantive Psalmic doctrine: the LORD Himself, in His personal presence, is the close-combat defensive armor the saint wears against the immediate personal attacks of the spiritual adversary. The buckler-doctrine is therefore not chiefly antiquarian vocabulary but the substantive doctrine of the LORD’s personal defensive presence appropriated by the saint’s trust in His name.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mágēn (shield, buckler), tsinnāh (large shield), and sōchērāh (small shield); the close-combat hand-shield of OT warfare, used by the Psalms as the imagery for the LORD Himself as the saint’s personal defensive presence appropriated by trust in His name; cousin to the NT shield of faith (Eph 6:16) in the comprehensive defensive protection of the spiritual warfare.

expand to see more

Hebrew mágēn (H4043) — shield, buckler (about 60 OT uses; often of the LORD Himself).

Hebrew tsinnāh (H6793) — large body-shield (about 20 OT uses).

Hebrew sōchērāh (H5507) — small shield (Ps 91:4, paired with shield).

Greek thureos (G2375) — large body-shield (Eph 6:16, the shield of faith; door-shaped, distinct from the smaller buckler).

"His truth shall be thy shield and buckler—Ps 91:4’s comprehensive shield-and-buckler pairing for the close-combat divine protection."

"Modernization drops buckler; the loss is small in vocabulary but real in nuance; biblical doctrine is the LORD Himself as personal-immediate-presence defensive armor, appropriated by trust in His name."
